title: Some Strategic Questions Shouldnt Be Answered
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that good leaders must learn to reject certain team questions outright, even when they're intellectually interesting, because chasing every inquiry slows decisions and adds needless complexity. It proposes a simple filter, "So What?", that tests whether the answer to any question would actually change a decision, approach, or behavior before resources are spent finding it. Questions that fail this test go into what the author calls the "Wouldn't-It-Be-Nice-To-Know" pile rather than triggering a deep dive. The piece frames this discipline as essential to decision speed, warning that "academic" questions are a common and underappreciated drain on team time and resources.
points: Not every interesting question deserves investment; the test is whether the answer would actually change a decision or behavior.
The "So What?" filter lets leaders quickly separate consequential questions from merely intellectually stimulating ones.
Questions that fail the "So What?" test should be deliberately set aside rather than pursued out of curiosity or thoroughness.
Chasing "academic" questions is a common, underappreciated way teams waste time and slow down decision-making.
quotes: Good leaders know that not all questions deserve the investment it takes to create a quality response.
Before investing in answering a question, good leaders ask, “So What?
In far too many cases, team members raise questions that when answered will make no difference in action or choice.
The rule is simple: If knowing the answer to any inquiry won’t alter the decision, modify the approach, or shift behavior—however intellectually stimulating it might be—then it needs to be ignored.
They accept that there is always more information and insight that would be intellectually satisfying to understand. But they value the time of those involved and the speed to decisions much more.
